title: history of the Cossacks
summary: The history of the Cossacks is marked by the emergence of semi-autonomous, militarized communities in the steppe regions north of the Black and Caspian seas, particularly influencing Ukraine's political and military landscape from the late medieval period onward.

sections.heading: Origins and Early History
paragraphs: The origins of the [[cossacks|Cossacks]] are subject to various theories, with some suggesting Slavic roots while others, including the Constitution of Pylyp Orlyk of 1710, propose Khazar origins. Modern scholars generally recognize a combination of Slavic and Turkic ancestry. Ivan Zabelin noted that ancient peoples, including the Borisphenites and Scythians, may have contributed to the Cossack lineage, supported by Cossack folklore and historical accounts.

Traditional historiography, influenced by post-imperial perspectives, dates the emergence of Cossacks to the 14th-15th centuries, while some non-mainstream theories suggest an earlier existence around 948 AD, when a leader named Kasak or Kazak reportedly defeated the Khazars in the Kuban area and established a state called Kazakia or Cossackia. The Cossacks, primarily East Slavs, were originally described in the 15th century as semi-independent Tatar groups residing along the [[dnieper|Dnieper River]], which flows through [[modern-history-of-ukraine|modern Ukraine]].

sections.heading: Cossack Societies and Territorial Organization
paragraphs: By the 16th century, Cossack societies had formed two main territorial organizations: [[zaporizhzhia|Zaporizhia]], located on the lower Dnieper [[coal-in-ukraine|in Ukraine]], and the Don Cossack State along the Don River. These communities operated as loose federations, maintaining independence from neighboring nations such as Poland, Russia, and the Tatars.

The Don Cossacks developed a unique warrior culture, engaging in raids for income and defending territories against the Golden Horde. They were recognized for their equestrian skills and were often employed as cavalry by Russian and [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]] leaders.

sections.heading: Interactions with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
paragraphs: During the 16th and 17th centuries, the Zaporizhian Cossacks became subjects of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. They utilized swift, maneuverable galleys known as chaiky for raids across the Black Sea, achieving notable military successes and gaining political influence.

Under the leadership of Petro Konashevych-Sahaidachny, the Cossacks sought to establish a Ukrainian nation, aligning with European powers against the Ottomans. Their military prowess was acknowledged even in Ottoman records, highlighting their fearlessness and skill in naval warfare.

sections.heading: Cossack Autonomy and Decline
paragraphs: The [[khmelnytsky-uprising|Khmelnytsky Uprising]] in the mid-17th century marked a significant turning point, leading to the Cossacks distancing themselves from the Commonwealth and coming under Russian influence through the [[treaty-of-pereyaslav|Treaty of Pereyaslav]] in 1654. This resulted in the establishment of the Left-bank [[ukraine|Ukraine]] and the eventual division of the Cossack nation into semi-autonomous entities within the Russian state.

By the late 18th century, Cossack autonomy diminished as Catherine II abolished these organizations, integrating the Hetmanate into the governorship of [[little-russia|Little Russia]] and Zaporozhia into New Russia. Those wishing to maintain their lifestyle migrated to territories under Ottoman or Austrian control, or moved to the Kuban region, where descendants of the Cossacks reside today.
